item.title: The 3 C’s of Strong Teams
item.description:
Teamwork

The 3 C’s of Strong Teams

How compassion, communication, and 'coming back' helps teams navigate conflict.

Posted August 9, 2026

Key points
  • Compassion includes an effort to uphold an awareness of other perspectives.
  • Communication involves conversations that are focused on clarity and connection rather than blame or judgment.
  • Coming back to commitments incorporates a balance of letting go and remembering the shared team mission.

Teams exist in myriad ways, from sports to specialized software development, from hospitals to high-tech organizations, and from medical professionals to media outlets. Many jobs, organizations, communities, and even families rely on well-functioning teams to get things accomplished effectively and efficiently.

Source: Matteo Vistocco/Unsplash

When a team is thriving in their unified goals and intentions, strengths can be maximized, the atmosphere is positive, and excellent work can be accomplished. People are connecting on a cohesive mission and doing their parts.

But if there is conflict, change, or any other kind of challenging interference in usual team roles and routines, the system can break down. This can lead to negativity, low morale, and potentially deleterious outcomes. This may start by affecting one person but often ripples onto others.

Conflict on a team can come from many different sources. Differences of opinion about how to proceed are a common issue; personality styles will often determine whether this leads to a reasonable negotiation or a stand-off - or whether a leader or manager will intervene. Sometimes the source of conflict comes from some team members overstepping their roles or boundaries, which can create confusion and resentment. Certain team members struggling to fulfill their responsibilities in the expected ways can also be a source of irritation and can cause significant strife and, in some cases, even safety issues.

The type of issue coming up on a specific team at a particular time will naturally dictate how resolution is ultimately achieved, but 3 broad recommendations can assist in creating more calm than conflict for most team clashes: compassion, communication and coming back to commitments. A variety of team examples are utilized as a means of further illustrating and enhancing the ideas in each of the domains.

Compassion

Having compassion for others, even when and sometimes especially when we are in conflict, can be highly valuable. If we are only thinking about why we are right and what someone else has done wrong, our perspective about the situation narrows considerably. By considering other possibilities, we are broadening our lens and giving ourselves a richer, deeper context.

article continues after advertisement
Source: Jakob Owens/Unsplash

Perspective on a situation matters. We often focus primarily on our own view, but stepping back to consider alternative viewpoints can help. If we are driving home and an emergency crew is rerouting us the long way around on a particular route, we might feel frustrated or inconvenienced; however, if we were the person who had the accident or a broken-down car, we would appreciate the traffic being rerouted. A player at one end of the soccer field might think the ball should have been easily blocked by their goalie, but the goalie sees firsthand that the ball is simply out of reach and too hard to stop.

When this compassion is upheld and experienced by others on the team, there is more space for resolution, increased trust, and potential for returning to a respectful stance. Just because a group of shipmates is experiencing the same change in weather on the same day from the same spot in the ocean, this doesn’t mean that all individuals will be doing the same things or having to respond to the weather pattern in the same way. We all have different roles and are on the lookout for different interventions.

There may not be agreement on how to resolve the issue, but having an attitude of compassion, benevolence and humility is key.

Communication

It is not uncommon for individuals to shut down and communicate less or less than ideally when there is conflict. Still, often this is exactly the time when more calm, clear, concrete communication strategies are needed. There may not always be a clear path forward, but the way remains foggy and murky without an opportunity for conversations.

Two athletes racing to the same ball is likely to add confusion and potentially collisions, but someone saying “I’ve got it” creates clarity and less unnecessary expenditure of energy. Software engineers letting each other know when the proposed fix didn’t work allows solutions to be explored, but seething anger, avoidance, or retaliative moves will delay the process of resolution. A disaster situation in a health center might uncover a number of procedures that are outdated and ineffective, and talking through these eventually will allow the next disaster situation to be approached differently.

Source: Yan Krukau/Pexels

Sorting through a conflict or a system failure together in a collaborative way is essential. Some groups engage in a team post-mortem following a major incident or breakdown as a means of reviewing what happened, understanding areas of improvement, and learning as much as possible from a negative event. For this to work effectively, the tone needs to be non-blaming, the review ideally includes items that went well, and action items are determined for each of the team members cooperatively.

article continues after advertisement

Humans aren’t mind-readers, nor do they respond well to dysregulated, angry, or blaming communication styles; instead, communication centered around clarity, curiosity, and connection work best.

Coming Back to Commitments

Coming back to the job, project or goal at hand is important. If the conflict has been caused by disagreement and the proposed resolution isn't considered to be ideal, coming back to the work despite the disagreement can be very difficult. Or if the clash has been more about boundaries and role overlap, coming back may entail getting back to one's usual job and trusting that other team members will do the same.

The process of letting go and letting be can be tricky, but attempting to over-function or to disengage are extremes that ultimately won’t help the team function well.

The first-chair violinist or the lead actor being sick on opening night might mean others have to shift their approach slightly for the night — and this can be stressful — but roles will resume when things are back to normal. When a chef has to take an emergency phone call, servers may have to pitch in a bit more to help get meals out to customers for a brief period of time; this isn’t the same as creating the menu or preparing the food, and the expectation is that each returns to their usual function once the chef steps back into the kitchen.

Source: Israyosoy S/Pexels

Like the ants in an anthill or the bees in a hive, members of a team all have their roles. There are times when the routine has to shift due to unexpected circumstances, such as a tornado that has crushed the home base, but repair and rebuilding can happen. And reconnecting around a shared purpose, value, or outcome can bring the team together again.

So, whether you are part of an athletic team, management team, treatment team, or any other type of group that has a mutual focus on a goal, remember the 3 C’s: Lead with compassion. Communicate collaboratively. Come back to commitments.

item.title: Why Your "Teachable Moments" Keep Backfiring
item.description:
Parenting

Why Your "Teachable Moments" Keep Backfiring

"Calm enough to listen" and "calm" are seemingly not the same thing.

Posted August 9, 2026

Key points
  • The moment right after a meltdown feels like the best time to teach the lesson. It's not.
  • Reopening the incident right then ("why did you do that," "we talked about this") doesn't teach anything.
  • Repair and teaching are two different jobs on two different timelines.

Here is a scenario I have heard recounted to me in various forms over many years. The screaming has stopped, and you feel your tense shoulders finally starting to relax. Your child is calm, or close to it. Maybe the setting is on the edge of the bed, or out on your deck, in a supermarket, or at a holiday dinner (yep, those are the most memorable ones). And here comes the pull that almost every parent feels: now's the time to explain why that was wrong—to talk it out/learn from it—while it's fresh. That instinct is nearly universal, and it's backward.

Appearing Calm Enough to Listen Does Not Mean Calm

Now consider the distinction almost no parent has had named for them: "appearing calm enough to listen" and "calm" are not the same thing. A nervous system that just finished a meltdown is depleted, not reset. Your child's (all the way from elementary through high school and sometimes adult children—and parents too) brain, post-meltdown, is closer to the exhausted quiet after a storm than a clear, engaged, teachable state. Reopening the incident right then ("Why did you do that?" "We talked about this.") doesn't teach the lesson. It asks a still-recovering brain to relive what it just spent five minutes surging over, and more often than not, it starts a second wave, smaller than the first but real, right when everyone thought the hard part was over.

I worked with a mother, Beth, whose six-year-old, Tess (all names in this post changed for privacy), would still be shaken right after a bedtime meltdown. Beth used to gently walk back through it by saying, "Remember how upset you got? Big kids can use their words," meaning well and trying to help her learn while it was fresh. Tess started crying again within a minute. Beth swapped this for lying quietly beside her for two minutes, without mentioning the incident. As Beth told me of this incident, she recounted that Tess fell asleep in a calm state, something the lecture had never once achieved.

When Silence Does Not Mean Defiant Shutdown

An eleven-year-old I worked with, Danny, went silent after his father asked, reasonably, "Why did you do that?" His father read the silence as defiance. It wasn't defiance, thought; it was just that Danny's nervous system didn't yet have an answer available. His father tried something smaller instead: no question that night, just "I'm not mad, let's talk tomorrow." Much to the dad's astonishment, Danny showed up at breakfast and explained the whole thing himself, unprompted.

The fix is a simple reframe: repair and teaching are two different jobs, on two different timelines. Repair is reconnection, showing your child that the relationship survived. Teaching belongs tomorrow, once there's a rested nervous system on both ends of the conversation. This exact sequencing is what my new book, 24 Hours to a Less Reactive Child, is built around: tonight's blowup, tomorrow morning's lesson, and why doing them in the wrong order keeps families stuck in the same fight on repeat.

article continues after advertisement

A Teenage Example With the Same Dynamic

Let's end this piece by highlighting Lana, a mother I worked with who caught herself mid-debrief with her sixteen-year-old daughter, Hope, after a blown curfew. Halfway through Lana's sentence, she noticed Hope's shoulders still shaking, and stopped: "Never mind. Tonight I just want you home safe. We'll talk tomorrow." Hope came to find Lana the next afternoon, calm, ready to actually talk. Knowing Hope well (from having several counseling sessions with her), I'm convinced she was open and approachable with her mom in a way the finished lecture never would have reached.

The Takeaway

Skipping the lecture isn't an excuse for skipping accountability. The boundary you held during the meltdown already did that work. The lesson isn't wasted by waiting. It's wasted by arriving too soon.
